title: Weeks 5-6 - Final Project
text:
Overview
Over the four instructional weeks you built a Pacific CI Portfolio - a living document capturing your work week by week. Now it’s time to assemble that portfolio into your final deliverable: a policy brief proposing how cyberinfrastructure could improve sustainability decision-making for your chosen Pacific island nation.
This project is designed to be completed by students of all technical backgrounds. Clear thinking, honest analysis, and understanding the specific use of real CI tools and datasets are the objectives of this course.

title: Weeks 5-6 - Final Project
text:
The Policy Brief
Your policy brief should be 3–5 pages and follow the five-section structure below. Each section connects directly to work you’ve already done in your portfolio.

Five-Section Structure

The sustainability problem Describe the challenge, who is affected, and why it matters now. Draw from your Week 1 data audit.
The CI landscape What data, tools, and infrastructure currently exist for this challenge - and what is critically missing? Draw from your Week 2 CI tool stack, Week 3 CI stack reflection, and Week 4 pipeline map.
The recommendation How could improved or better-used cyberinfrastructure improve decision-making for this challenge? Be specific - name tools, platforms, or data types. Draw from Weeks 3 and 4.
Limitations and equity concerns What could go wrong? What access, sovereignty, or capacity barriers apply? Who might be excluded from the solution you’re proposing?
Call to action What should a specific, named decision-maker do - and by when?

title: Weeks 5-6 - Final Project
section: What Makes a Strong Policy Brief
text:
What Makes a Strong Policy Brief


🏝️ Specific and grounded Names a specific Pacific island nation and a specific sustainability challenge - not a general topic.


🛠️ Uses real tools References at least two real CI tools, datasets, or platforms encountered during the course.


🔍 Identifies a concrete gap Names a specific CI gap - not just “more data is needed” but what data, held by whom, used by whom.


⚖️ Acknowledges equity Includes a frank limitations section acknowledging equity, access, or sovereignty concerns.


📢 Clear call to action Ends with a call to action addressed to a real, named decision-maker - not a generic recommendation.


📁 Builds on your portfolio Draws visibly from your Pacific CI Portfolio - the brief should feel earned, not written from scratch.

title: Weeks 5-6 - Final Project
section: How Your Portfolio Feeds Into the Brief
text:

Portfolio section
Feeds into brief as…

title: Weeks 5-6 - Final Project
text:
The Presentation
Along with your policy brief, you will record a 5-minute video presentation summarizing your work. Slides are recommended but not required.

Your presentation should cover:

Self-introduction (name, background, etc.)
Your island country and sustainability challenge - why you chose it
The CI landscape - what exists and what’s missing
Your recommendation - what CI could improve decision-making and how
Your call to action - who should do what, and by when

Recording tips:

Use Zoom, Loom, or any screen recording tool you’re comfortable with
If using slides, keep them simple
Speak clearly and at a natural pace - 5 minutes goes faster than you think
Submit your video link or file in Google Classroom

title: Week 3 - Accessing CI and How It Works
text:
Module 3A



The National Science Foundation (NSF) has invested millions of dollars in cyberinfrastructure that benefits the Pacific. A $4.5 million grant to the University of Hawaiʻi built the fiber optic research network connections linking Guam, American Samoa, Australia, New Zealand, and the US mainland. A more recent NSF award funds the Cyberinfrastructure Pacific Professionals (CI-PP) project - training and supporting researchers and students in advanced CI across Hawaiʻi, Guam, and US-Affiliated Pacific Islands.
This infrastructure didn’t build itself. It exists because researchers made the case, wrote the proposals, and connected Pacific institutions to the national CI ecosystem. This module introduces you to that ecosystem - what NSF funds, what’s available, and how Pacific researchers have accessed it.

📖 Read more: Cyberinfrastructure Pacific Professionals (CI-PP) - learn more about NSF-funded CI work supporting researchers and students across Hawaiʻi, Guam, and US-Affiliated Pacific Islands.

Use the Field of Science filter to browse projects relevant to your island’s sustainability challenge. Try fields like:

title: Week 3 - Accessing CI and How It Works
text:
How It Works

Module 3B


🪝 Hook
In April 2026, Super Typhoon Sinlaku formed in the western Pacific and rapidly grew to a Category 5, 185-mph storm. It first hit Chuuk in the Federated States of Micronesia, then struck Saipan and Tinian in the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands. The storm flipped cars, toppled utility poles, and ripped away tin roofs - leaving much of Saipan without power.
The forecasters who tracked Sinlaku’s path provided advanced noticed to the communities - not because they were lucky, but because high-performance computing infrastructure was running models too large for any local machine to handle and processing data from satellites and weather stations in real time.
This module opens that black box. How does cloud computing work? What is HPC and when do you need it? And how is this infrastructure already being used to support Pacific sustainability research?



🎬 Lecture Video

How It Works - Lecture Video
Your lecture video will go here. To embed a YouTube video, replace this block with:
{=html} <iframe width="100%" height="415" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/YOUR-VIDEO-ID"  title="How It Works" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen></iframe>




🪸 Hands-On Use Case - Allen Coral Atlas
The Allen Coral Atlas uses machine learning on cloud infrastructure to map coral reef health across the entire Pacific - a task that would be impossible to do manually at this scale. It’s a powerful example of what cloud computing and ML make possible for Pacific sustainability research.

Your task this module:
Visit the Allen Coral Atlas and explore reef health for your chosen island country.
What to look for:

Find your island - what does the reef health map show?
Find one reef area showing change or degradation
Click into the data - what satellite imagery and timeframes are available?
Think about the infrastructure behind it: what data fed this model, and what computing power runs it?



📖 Explore: NASA Pacific Flooding Analysis Tool - interactive tool showing projected high-tide flooding frequency and extent for Pacific island locations under different sea-level rise scenarios.




📋 Mini Assignment - CI Stack Reflection

Week 3 Assignment - CI Stack Reflection
Using the Allen Coral Atlas, answer the following:
Allen Coral Atlas:

What do you see? Describe the reef health map for your island — what does it show about the current state of the reefs?
What change can you identify? Find one area showing reef degradation or bleaching. What does the Atlas tell you about it?
Who built this and how? Visit the Attribution page and Partners page. Summarize what data was used to build this tool and who worked together to make it happen.
What decision could this inform? Name one specific decision a marine manager, government official, or community leader in your island could make using this map.
What’s missing? What does this tool not tell you that a decision-maker would still need to know?

Add your responses to the Week 3 section of your Pacific CI Portfolio Google Doc and submit the link in Google Classroom.
→ Submit Week 3 Assignment in Google Classroom

title: Cyberinfrastructure Fundamentals
text:
What is this course about?
Pacific Islands are on the front lines of climate change - rising seas, intensifying typhoons, and shrinking freshwater supplies threaten communities across the region. To address these challenges, what tools, resources, and data exist?
This course introduces cyberinfrastructure - the hardware, software, data systems, networks, and human capacity that power modern research - and explores how it can be leveraged for sustainability decision-making in Small Island Developing States (SIDS) and the Pacific region.
No coding experience required. Just curiosity and a commitment to the Pacific.

title: Week 1 - Getting Started
text:
CI Foundations

Module 1B


🪝 Hook
Pacific island communities are already leading in sustainability and climate action - combining traditional knowledge, local expertise, and scientific tools to address some of the world’s most urgent sustainability challenges. But accessing the data and computational tools that could support that work isn’t always straightforward.
This module introduces cyberinfrastructure - a powerful set of tools that can help bridge the gap between the data that exists and the decisions that need to be made.

“Pacific Islanders are leading climate action and combining their own systems of knowledge with western science to implement locally relevant climate solutions.” - Frontiers in Marine Science, 2019


📖 Recommended video: Definition of Cyberinfrastructure - Watch this video for a brief overview of what cyberinfrastructure is.




🎬 Lecture Video

CI Foundations - Lecture Video
Your lecture video will go here. To embed a YouTube video, replace this block with:
{=html} <iframe width="100%" height="415" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/YOUR-VIDEO-ID"  title="CI Foundations" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen></iframe>




Hands-On Use Case - Pacific Data Hub
The Pacific Data Hub is a regional cyberinfrastructure platform aggregating climate, fisheries, ocean, and demographic data from 20+ Pacific nations. This is cyberinfrastructure in action - a shared regional platform that gives researchers and decision-makers across the Pacific access to data they couldn’t build or maintain independently.

Your task this week:
Visit pacificdata.org and spend 10-20 minutes exploring before completing the mini assignment below.
What to look for:

What kinds of data are available for the different islands?
Who collected it and when was it last updated?
What sustainability challenges does it connect to?
What feels missing?





📋 Mini Assignment - Data Audit

Week 1 Assignment - Data Audit
Using the Pacific Data Hub, choose one Pacific island country - this will be your focus for all four portfolio entries throughout the course. Find two datasets tied to a sustainability challenge (sea level, freshwater, fisheries, coral reefs, food security, or another challenge relevant to your island).
For each dataset, answer these four prompts:

Decision value: What specific question could a local planner, official, or community leader answer using this data?
Who decides: Name one real role who would use this - e.g. fisheries officer, disaster risk manager, mayor.
Data gap: What is missing, outdated, or too coarse to make that decision confidently?
Infrastructure gap: Is the gap a data problem, a connectivity problem, a capacity problem - or all three?

Add your responses to the Week 1 section of your Pacific CI Portfolio Google Doc. When you’re done, submit your portfolio link in Google Classroom.
→ Submit Week 1 Assignment in Google Classroom




Discussion Prompt
This week’s second discussion in Google Classroom.

Before we dive in - what do you think of when you hear the word ‘cyberinfrastructure’? No wrong answers. Just your honest first impression.

Respond in 2–3 sentences minimum.
→ Go to Week 1 Discussion in Google Classroom



Closing Thoughts

The Pacific Data Hub now gives a fisheries officer in Nauru access to regional ocean data that would have taken weeks to gather a decade ago. That’s what shared cyberinfrastructure makes possible - and you’re just getting started.

title: Week 2 - The Pacific and CI Tools
text:
Module 2A



Small Island Developing States make up less than 1% of global greenhouse gas emissions - yet they face some of the most severe consequences of climate change. Rising seas, intensifying storms, shrinking freshwater supplies, and collapsing fisheries aren’t abstract future risks for Pacific communities. They are present-day realities.
But Pacific island nations are not passive victims. They are active leaders in sustainability action - combining traditional ecological knowledge, community-based approaches, and scientific tools to adapt and respond. The question this module explores is: what does sustainability actually mean in this context, and how does data and cyberinfrastructure affect those efforts?

📖 Recommended reading: About Small Island Developing States (SIDS) - Read to learn about what the Small Island Developing States are, who is it home to, challenges they face, and more.






Sustainability in the Pacific - Lecture Video
Your lecture video will go here. To embed a YouTube video, replace this block with:
{=html} <iframe width="100%" height="415" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/YOUR-VIDEO-ID"  title="Sustainability in the Pacific" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen></iframe>





The UNDP SIDS Data Platform is a cyberinfrastructure tool built specifically for Small Island Developing States - including country-level sustainability indicators, a GIS portal with geospatial datasets, and a Multidimensional Vulnerability Index across all SIDS regions including the Pacific.

Your task this module:
Visit the UNDP SIDS Data Platform and explore the data available for your chosen Pacific island country.
What to look for:

Find your island country’s profile - what sustainability indicators are tracked?
Look at the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index (MVI) - where does your island rank and why?
What data is missing or flagged as unavailable for your island?
How does this platform compare to the Pacific Data Hub you explored in Week 1?

🌊 Hands-On Use Case - PacIOOS
PacIOOS (Pacific Islands Ocean Observing System) is a real-time ocean and coastal monitoring network - buoys, wave sensors, and tide gauges - operating across Hawaiʻi and the Pacific Islands. It’s a working example of a CI tool stack in action: sensors collect data, transmit it via satellite, store it in the cloud, and visualize it in a live dashboard accessible from any browser.

Your task this module:
Visit the PacIOOS data viewer and explore sensor data near your chosen island country.
What to look for:

Find a sensor feed relevant to a sustainability challenge your island faces (may not include data for your specific island, but beneficial to explore what’s out there!)
What does the data show - what is being measured and how often?
Can you find any gaps in coverage near your island?
How does the data get from the sensor to your screen? Think about the CI stack concept from the lecture.



📖 Explore further: Science Gateways - check out some of the NSF-funded science gateways available and learn how to use them.




📋 Mini Assignment - CI Tool Stack

Week 2 Assignment - CI Tool Stack
Using what you explored in the PacIOOS hands-on use case and the lecture, design a simple CI tool stack for the sustainability challenge from Week 1 for your chosen island country.
Complete the five-field template:

Sustainability challenge: What problem are you monitoring? (e.g. coastal erosion in Tuvalu)
What to measure: Which variables matter? (e.g. wave height, sea surface temperature, population)
Tool or sensor type: What would collect or process this data? (e.g. coastal buoy, satellite imagery, open data portal)
Data transmission: How does data get from the source to a usable format? (e.g. satellite uplink, cloud storage, open API)
Constraint or trade-off: One real infrastructure barrier affecting your design (e.g. limited bandwidth, no reliable power grid, no institutional email for tool access)

title: Week 4 - From Data to Decisions
text:
Module 4



Imagine you have access to sea level data, reef health maps, and climate projections for your island. Now, imagine sitting across from a local official who has to decide where to invest limited infrastructure funds. What do you actually say?
This is the last-mile problem - the gap between what cyberinfrastructure produces and what decision-makers can actually use. Data alone doesn’t make decisions. Someone has to translate it, communicate it, and connect it to action. This module is about that gap - and how to bridge it.





Data to Decisions - Lecture Video
Your lecture video will go here. To embed a YouTube video, replace this block with:
{=html} <iframe width="100%" height="415" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/YOUR-VIDEO-ID"  title="Data to Decisions" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen></iframe>


Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) are climate commitments each country submits under the Paris Agreement — outlining what they plan to do to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. The Regional Pacific NDC Hub supports 14 Pacific island nations in developing and implementing these plans, and their website brings together country profiles, climate commitments, and implementation resources in one place.
NDCs are a real example of the last-mile problem in action — they take scientific data and climate projections and translate them into government commitments and policy priorities.

Your task this module:
Visit the Regional Pacific NDC Hub and explore resources for your chosen island country.
What to look for:

Does your island country have an NDC profile or resources on the hub?
What sustainability priorities and climate commitments are highlighted?
What data or evidence is referenced to support those commitments? (Read some of the documents under the country’s profile.)
How does the language in these documents connect to the CI tools and data you’ve explored in previous weeks?

If your island country is not one of the 14 Hub member countries, browse the profile of the geographically closest member country and note the similarities and differences.


📖 Read more: CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance — approximately 5 pages. Consider how each principle applies to Pacific data governance contexts.






Week 4 Assignment - Stakeholder + CI Pipeline Map
For your chosen island country and sustainability challenge, produce a structured map/document covering the following five areas. This map becomes the evidence section of your policy brief in Weeks 5 and 6 - so be as specific and honest as you can. Identifying gaps is just as valuable as identifying what exists.

The sustainability problem: One clear sentence describing the challenge and who is affected.
Key decision-makers: Who are the 2-3 people or institutions that make decisions about this challenge? (e.g. Ministry of Environment, village council, regional fisheries body)
CI that currently exists: What data, platforms, or models are already available for this challenge? Reference tools or datasets you’ve encountered in Weeks 1-3. Research and look for more CI tools that exist online.
What is missing: What CI gap most limits good decision-making here? Be specific - not just “more data” but what kind, held by whom, used by whom.
Who is excluded: Who is affected by this sustainability challenge but left out of the data collection or the decision-making process?

Add your responses to the Week 4 section of your Pacific CI Portfolio Google Doc and submit the link in Google Classroom.
→ Submit Week 4 Assignment in Google Classroom





This week’s discussion is in Google Classroom.

For the assignment, you mapped who is excluded from the data or the decision. Did this surpise you - and what does it tell you about where cyberinfrastructure needs to go next in the Pacific?

Respond in 2–3 sentences.
→ Go to Week 4 Discussion in Google Classroom





The gap between data and decisions is where cyberinfrastructure meets policy - and where you can make the most difference. Your policy brief starts now. You already have everything you need.
